entry.title: How to Review Your Kid’s Whole Season in 20 Minutes

link.title: How to Review Your Kid’s Whole Season in 20 Minutes

entry.content:
A season review takes about twenty minutes and needs three things: one comparison, three questions, and two sentences written down somewhere you’ll actually find them next season.

The comparison is your kid’s first four games against their last four. The questions get asked at the kitchen bench, not in the car. The two sentences are what you both want to be different next year.

It works whether you recorded every game or none of them, and the version for parents who tracked nothing is more useful than no review at all, so start there if that’s you.

What a season review is actually for

Nobody needs to grade an eleven-year-old’s winter. The point is to pin down what changed while the evidence still exists.

By March you’ll remember two things about this season: the best game and the worst umpire. Twelve rounds of steady, unglamorous improvement will have quietly evaporated.

Your kid can’t see it either. Kids measure themselves against the best player on the team, today. Nobody measures themselves against who they were in April on their own. Somebody has to point at the two ends and show them the gap.

The three questions worth asking your kid

Ask about a week after the last game. If it ended badly, give it longer.

  1. “What can you do now that you couldn’t do in the first game?” They will say “dunno”. Wait. If the silence gets long, prime it with something you noticed, then let them take it over.
  2. “What was the best thing that happened this year?” It’s almost never a goal. Usually a moment, and often one you didn’t see. Let it be whatever it is, even if it’s the bus trip to the carnival.
  3. “What do you want to be better at next year?” Their answer, not yours. Write it in their words, including the wrong words.

Three questions is the whole list. If you find yourself on question seven, you’ve stopped reviewing and started coaching.

How to do this if you tracked nothing all season

This is most parents. You have more than you think.

Your camera roll, sorted by date. Open the first game and the last game side by side. Look at where they’re standing when the ball is somewhere else, and who they’re standing next to. You’ll see things you didn’t notice live.

The team group chat. Scroll back to April. Match reports, scores, team lists, the week they got moved into the ruck. It’s a season diary written by twenty-two people who didn’t know they were writing one.

Your own memory, but only against a prompt. “How did he play this year” gets you nothing. “What was he doing in round two that he’d stopped doing by round ten” gets you an answer.

That gives you a story rather than numbers, and the story is what the conversation runs on. What it won’t tell you is whether his disposals, every time he touched the ball by kick or handball, went up or down. Nothing reconstructs that after the fact.

How to do this if you did track: what to look at, what to ignore

Look at disposals, because volume is where junior improvement shows up first. Tackles and contested involvements, because effort stats move earliest, often a month before anything else does. Game time, because it’s the context for every other number on the page.

Ignore goals, which are mostly a story about position and who else is on the field. Any single game, which tells you about the weather. And the season average, which sits in the middle of the range and hides the exact thing you’re looking for.

As for recording it in the first place, three options work. A notes app is free and perfectly good, as long as you remember to open it. A paper tally on the back of the fixture works beautifully and then goes through the wash. A stats app does the counting and the remembering for you.

ScorX is the third kind. You tap what you see while the game is running, and it keeps a game-by-game record for that player, so in September you open one screen and see the shape of the season instead of trying to recall it. The free version covers one player in one sport and the data stays on your phone.

The one comparison that matters: first four games against last four

Not round by round. Junior game-to-game variation is enormous, and one game tells you about the ground conditions. Four games starts to tell you about the kid. The season average is no better, because you want the difference between the two ends, not the middle.

Add up the first four, add up the last four, and put them next to each other.

What counts as real is a change you’d notice without squinting. Nine disposals a game going to eleven is noise. Nine going to sixteen is a different player.

If the numbers went sideways or backwards, slow down before you read anything into it. Moving up an age group flattens everything for about six weeks. So does a position change, a coach who started rotating them through the midfield, and a growth spurt that arrived in July. Write down what changed around them first, then decide what the numbers mean.

What to write down so next season starts somewhere

Two sentences. One in their words, one in yours.

Ollie: “I want to get better at kicking with my left.” Me: he stopped hiding at the back of packs around round six. Keep that going.

Put it in your notes app and pin it, or on the front page of next year’s fixture. Somewhere you’ll find it in 5 months, which is not a piece of paper in the kitchen drawer. The best option is log it as a development goal in an app like ScorX.

The payoff comes at the first training session next season, when they ask what they should be working on and you have an answer that came out of their own mouth five months ago. Much better than the one you make up in the car park.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do you review a junior sport season with your child?

Set aside twenty minutes about a week after the last game, once the result has stopped stinging. Do three things. Compare their first four games to their last four, using whatever you have, which is recorded stats if you tracked them and photos and match reports if you didn’t. Ask three questions. What can you do now that you couldn’t do in the first game? What was the best thing that happened? What do you want to be better at next year? Then write two sentences down, one in their words and one in yours, and put them somewhere you’ll find them when pre-season starts.

How long should a season review take?

Twenty minutes. If it’s stretched to an hour it has turned into a performance review, and an eleven-year-old doesn’t need one of those.

What if my kid doesn’t want to talk about it?

Leave it a fortnight and try again sideways, in the car on the way to something that has nothing to do with footy. If they still don’t want to, do your half on your own and keep the note. The conversation can happen in February.

Should I show my kid their stats?

Show them the two ends, unless they are keen on the detail. “Round two you had nine touches, round twelve you had sixteen” lands. A full table doesn’t, and it invites them to compare their numbers to their teammates’, which is the one thing a season review should never turn into.

ScorX is free to download. If this year’s review came up thinner than you’d like, round 1 is where that gets fixed.

entry.title: Why the Best Game of the Season Often Goes Uncelebrated

link.title: Why the Best Game of the Season Often Goes Uncelebrated

entry.content:
Your kid has the best game of the season. Five goals, an intercept, the kind of afternoon you actually want people to know about. And what do you do with it? You text three people “she played SO well today” and that’s it. Gone by Monday.

This isn’t a discipline problem. You’re not lazy, and you’re not the only parent standing on the sideline thinking “someone should make this look like something.” The truth is there’s never been an easy way to turn a good game into something worth sending. At least not without an hour, a laptop, and some Canva skills.

Why a good game deserves better than a group text

A scoreline in a group chat disappears in about four seconds of scrolling. It doesn’t capture what actually happened. Today she read the ball, that he backed himself for once, that the whole team lifted in the last quarter. None of that survives “3-1, good win today.”

Compare that to a photo from a wedding, a birthday, a work milestone. Those moments get a graphic, a card, something with a bit of polish, because someone decided they were worth the extra ten minutes. A great game from your kid rarely gets the same treatment, and it’s not because it matters less. It’s because nobody’s worked out how to make it easy.

What’s actually stopping parents from sharing it properly

Three things, and they’re not about motivation.

Time. You’re standing on a sideline holding a coffee, not sitting at a desk with design software open. Whatever you make has to happen in the ten minutes between full-time and the car ride home, or it doesn’t happen.

Skill. Canva templates exist, sure. They also take twenty minutes to find, resize, and fill in. Also most of them were built for birthday invites, not sport. You end up with something that looks close but not quite right, which somehow feels worse than not trying.

Access. The graphics you see from AFLW broadcasts, from college programs overseas, from the polished stuff on a club’s Instagram, that’s built by someone with a design team and licensed templates. It was never meant for a Tuesday night netball game in a suburban gym. Pro-level graphics were genuinely out of reach for a parent with a phone and five minutes.

That third one is the real gap. It’s not that parents don’t want to celebrate a good performance properly. It’s that the tools capable of doing it well have, until recently, belonged to people with a production budget.

What a decent sports graphics generator actually needs to do

It shouldn’t just add features. It should remove steps. The job is: take what actually happened in the game. The stats, the score, the moment, and turn it into something that looks intentional, in about as long as it takes to leave the car park.

That means no template hunting, no resizing, no typing scores in by hand after the fact. If a parent has to open a second app or dig up a photo to make it work, it’s already lost the ten-minute window it had to be useful.

This is where ScorX earns its mention, and it’s a fair one: it was built around exactly this gap. You record the game as it happens. A tackle here, a goal there, then at full-time it turns straight into a shareable card, stats and all. No template. No app-switching. It’s the same graphic quality you’d expect from a broadcast, generated from the numbers you were already tracking from the sideline.

It doesn’t replace the group chat. It just gives the group chat something worth sending. A final-score card, a progress update mid-game, or a card built around one kid’s individual performance when that’s the story of the day.

The bit that actually matters

None of this is really about graphics. It’s about a kid finishing a genuinely good game and having something to point to afterwards that isn’t just a feeling. “You played well” fades. A card with the actual numbers on it doesn’t.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do you make a shareable sports graphic for a kid’s game?

The fastest way is an app that turns the stats you’re already tracking into a graphic automatically, rather than building one from scratch afterwards. Recording basic stats during the game, score, key moments, individual touches, means the graphic exists the second the final whistle goes, instead of requiring a separate design step later that night. Tools like Canva work if you have twenty minutes and know what you’re doing with templates, but they weren’t built for sport specifically, so you end up manually entering scores and resizing text boxes. A sports-specific graphics generator like ScorX skips that step entirely: the card is built from the live data, so it’s ready to share within seconds of the game ending, whether that’s a mid-game score update, a final result, or a card celebrating one player’s performance.

Do I need any design skill to make these look good?

No. The whole point of a purpose-built tool is that the layout, colours, and typography are already handled — you’re filling in game data, not designing a graphic.

Can I share the score as the game is happening, not just at the end?

Yes, if the app you’re using supports live tracking. That’s what makes it different from a graphic you build after the fact — you can share an update at any time as well as the final result.

Is this only useful for the kids who are already the star player?

No — that’s actually the opposite of the point. A card built from real stats gives every kid something concrete to point to, not just the ones who score. Effort, tackles, and involvement all show up, not just goals.

entry.title: Playing in a Grand Final Is Rarer Than It Feels

link.title: Playing in a Grand Final Is Rarer Than It Feels

entry.content:
If your boy or girl is playing in a grand final this month, they’re doing something most kids who play community sport never get to do. For a lot of them it’s also a first. Finals only become standard from Under 13, so this may be the first season a result has ever counted at all, let alone gone all the way to a granny.

It’s easy to miss how rare that actually is, mostly because grand final week is so busy. There’s the training, the group chat blowing up, the “have you seen my mouthguard” of it all. Somewhere in the logistics, the fact that this particular event is genuinely uncommon gets lost.

How rare is a grand final, actually?

Do the maths on any local competition and it’s stark. In a typical junior AFL grade, eight to twelve teams play all season, and exactly two of them run out on grand final day. That’s one team in four or five, most years, and that’s before you account for the seasons a good side gets knocked out the week before.

Stretch that across a whole junior career and a kid who makes even one grand final has beaten odds that most of their teammates over the years didn’t. Two grannies across a junior career is a genuinely good run. Some very good players, kids who train hard and improve every season, go through their entire time at a club without one.

The game they’ll still be talking about at eighteen

Here’s the part that’s easy to undersell at thirteen. Grand finals are the games that stick. Not every good game, not every good season, but the grand final specifically. Ask any adult who played junior sport what they remember and it’s rarely a good Round 9. It’s the final. The score, who kicked what, who got a guernsey they didn’t expect.

That’s not just nostalgia talking. It’s the one day the whole team experienced together, at the same intensity, all wanting the exact same outcome. Regular season doesn’t build stories like that. Grand finals do.

Your kid’s teammates will bring this game up for years. At a reunion, in a group chat on the anniversary, randomly at training in three seasons’ time when someone mentions the ground. “Remember the grand final” is a sentence that gets said a lot longer than “remember Round 9.”

Why this is worth telling your kid, carefully

There’s a difference between adding pressure and adding meaning. “This is huge, don’t let the team down” is pressure. “Not everyone gets to do this, and you’ll be talking about it for years” is meaning, and they can usually tell the two apart.

The version that lands well is small and specific, said once rather than repeated all week. Something like: “however Saturday goes, this is one you’ll be telling stories about.” At this age it doesn’t need explaining or dwelling on. Say it, mean it, move on. Over-explaining it gets you an eye roll and undoes the point.

How to help them actually feel it, not just survive it

Most grand final advice is about managing nerves, which matters, but it treats the day like something to get through. A day this uncommon is also worth treating like something to be in, not just endure.

At this age that mostly means getting out of the way. Let them have their pre-game time with teammates rather than hovering. Teens process a big day through their mates more than through their parents, and that’s exactly as it should be. Your job is logistics and a calm car trip, not narration.

It’s also worth actually keeping something from the day, even if your kid rolls their eyes at the idea in the moment. A photo, a scoreline, a card with what they actually did on it. They may not want it at thirteen. They will absolutely want it later, when the details of the day have gone fuzzy and they’re the one telling the “remember the grand final” story. That’s a small part of what ScorX is for: giving a day like this something to point back to that isn’t just a memory getting less reliable every season.

Frequently Asked Questions

How rare is it for a kid to play in a grand final?

Rarer than grand final week usually makes it feel. In a typical junior competition with eight to twelve teams, only two reach the grand final each season, meaning most players in most years don’t get there at all. For a 13 year old specifically it can also be a genuine first, since finals only become standard from Under 13 in most junior AFL competitions. Across a full junior career, making even one grand final is a good outcome, and plenty of strong, hardworking players go through their whole time at a club without one. None of this is meant to add weight to the day. It’s the opposite: knowing how uncommon it is can help both parents and kids notice and enjoy it while it’s actually happening, and understand why it’s the game teammates will still be bringing up years from now, long after most of the season has been forgotten.

Does missing out on a grand final mean a team had a bad season?

No. Most teams in most competitions don’t make the grand final in any given year, including plenty of teams that improved a lot and had a genuinely good season by any measure that isn’t the ladder.

How do I tell my kid that the grand final is a big deal without adding pressure?

Keep it brief, specific and said once, not repeated all week. Something like “you’ll be talking about this one for years” lands as meaning rather than pressure, especially delivered without any mention of the result attached to it.

Why do grand finals get remembered more than regular season games?

They’re the one day the whole team wants the exact same outcome at the same intensity, which builds a shared story in a way an ordinary round rarely does. That’s why “remember the grand final” tends to outlast almost every other memory from a junior sporting career.

ScorX is free to download. If grand final day is coming up, it’s worth having something to look back on beyond the final score.

entry.title: What to Say to Your Kid After They Lose a Final

link.title: What to Say to Your Kid After They Lose a Final

entry.content:
Your kid just lost a final. They’re in the back seat, hood up, not talking. You have about eight minutes of driving to work out what to do with that.

Here’s the part nobody warns you about. The game is not the thing they’ll remember. The car is.

That’s the actual problem, and it’s harder than it looks. You aren’t deciding what to say about the game. You’re deciding whether the next ten minutes turn a bad Saturday into a bad memory. Most of us are guessing, and most of us guess by talking too much.

Why this one lands harder than you expected

There’s a good chance this is the first final your kid has ever lost, and not because they’ve been winning them.

Under the AFL’s junior rules there are no finals at all through to under-11s. No ladders, no premiership points, no scores recorded. The handbook is blunt about it: for under-8 through under-11, the line reads “no scores, ladders or finals.” Finals only become possible at under-12, and even then it’s left to each league to decide. From under-13 they’re standard.

So a kid who just lost their first final has played four or five seasons where the result genuinely did not count, followed by one where it suddenly did. Nobody sat them down and explained the switch. They just turned up one Saturday and the scoreboard mattered.

That’s worth holding onto on the drive home. They’re not being dramatic. They’re feeling something for the first time, without any practice at it.

Why the drive home is the part they’ll remember

Bruce Brown and Rob Miller, two American coaches who run a program called Proactive Coaching, spent about three decades asking college athletes one question: what’s your worst memory from playing junior and school sport?

The most common answer wasn’t a loss. It wasn’t an injury, or a coach, or getting dropped.

It was the ride home from games with their parents.

That should land uncomfortably, because none of those parents were being cruel. They were debriefing. They were being helpful. They were filling a silence that felt unbearable to them and was probably fine for the kid.

The same athletes were asked what their parents said that actually made them feel good. The answer was six words: I love to watch you play.

Not a strategy. Not encouragement. Just the plain fact that watching them was the good part.

What to say in the first ten minutes

Almost nothing. That’s the honest answer.

The first ten minutes after a loss are not a conversation. They’re a recovery period, and a twelve-year-old is not going to be reasonable during one. Neither are you, if we’re being fair about it.

So keep it to three things.

  1. Name the feeling without fixing it. “That was a rough one.” “You wanted that.” That’s it. Don’t add a “but”.
  2. Say the six words, or your own version. “I love watching you play.” It sounds too simple to work. It works because it isn’t conditional on the result, and they can tell.
  3. Ask about food. Genuinely. “Are you starving?” is a better question than anything about the third quarter, and it gives them something easy to answer while they sort themselves out.

Then stop. Put the radio on. Let the silence be a normal silence instead of a loaded one.

If they want to talk, they’ll start. Kids almost always do, about eleven minutes in, usually about something that seems completely unrelated.

What to skip entirely

The umpire. Even if the umpire was terrible. Especially if the umpire was terrible. The moment you hand your kid an external reason for the loss, you’ve taught them that results happen to them rather than because of anything they did. That’s a much more expensive lesson than one final.

The coaching. You’ve watched every game this season and you have opinions. Save them. The car is not a review, and you are not the coach.

The “at least”. “At least you made the finals.” “At least you got a couple of kicks.” Every “at least” is a small correction of how they’re allowed to feel, and they hear it as one.

The silver lining, delivered immediately. There is one. It’s real. It’ll still be there on Tuesday. Delivered eight minutes after the siren, it just sounds like you weren’t paying attention.

When to actually talk about the game

Sport psychologists have a rough rule for this: wait 24 hours before you talk about what went wrong. The Association for Applied Sport Psychology puts it plainly in its guidance for parents. Straight after a game, a young athlete is still coming down from it, and nothing said in that window lands the way you meant it.

At junior level I’d push it out further. Two days is better. By Monday afternoon the loss has stopped being an emotional event and started being a thing that happened.

When you do talk about it, don’t open with the final. Open wider.

Ask them what they got better at this year. Ask what they can do now that they couldn’t in March. Most kids can’t answer that on their own, which is the frustrating bit. They finish fifteen games with a vague sense they improved and nothing they can point to, so a loss in the last one feels like the whole story.

It isn’t. But you have to be able to show them that, not just tell them.

What this looks like at twelve versus sixteen

Twelve to thirteen. This is the hard one, because it’s usually their first. Old enough to understand what a final means, not old enough to have any perspective on it. They may cry and then be furious that they cried. Say less, sit closer, don’t make eye contact in the mirror.

Fourteen to fifteen. They’ve lost one before, which helps less than you’d think. This is the age where the loss gets attached to a story about themselves, so listen for “I’m just not good enough” and take that seriously later in the week rather than arguing with it in the car.

Sixteen and up. They want to be left alone and then they want to talk, in that order, and the gap between the two is unpredictable. Your job is to still be available at 9pm when it arrives.

Whatever age they are, the loss will shrink. What makes it shrink faster is having something to put next to it. That’s the whole reason ScorX exists: a season your kid can actually see, so the last game stops being the only one that counts.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should you say to your child after they lose a final?

Say very little, and make almost none of it about the game. In the first ten minutes, name the feeling without trying to fix it. Something like “that was a rough one” or “you really wanted that” tells them you were paying attention without asking them to process anything yet. Then say a version of “I love watching you play”, which is the phrase college athletes most often name as the thing that helped, because it isn’t conditional on how they went. Then offer them food and stop talking. Let the silence be ordinary. Avoid the umpire, avoid coaching points, and avoid any sentence starting with “at least”, because each one quietly corrects how they’re allowed to feel. Save the real conversation for two days later, when the loss has stopped being an emotional event and turned into something that just happened.

What age do junior AFL players start playing finals?

Under-12 at the earliest, and it’s each league’s decision. The AFL’s junior rules specify no scores, ladders or finals through to under-11s. Finals are standard from under-13.

Should you talk about the game on the drive home at all?

Only if they start it. If they do, follow their lead and stay off analysis. Answering their questions is fine. Introducing your own isn’t.

What if my child doesn’t want to talk at all?

That’s a normal response, not a worrying one. Stay nearby, keep the evening ordinary, and let them come to you. Most kids do, usually at a strange hour and about something apparently unrelated.

Is it alright to be disappointed too?

Yes, and pretending otherwise doesn’t fool them. Just make sure your disappointment is clearly about the result and not about them. Kids read that difference instantly, and they read it in your face before they read it in your words.

ScorX is free to download. Track next season from round one and your kid will finish it with more than a feeling.

entry.title: How to Prepare Your Kid for a Footy Final

link.title: How to Prepare Your Kid for a Footy Final

entry.content:
Your kid made finals. Somewhere between Monday and Saturday, you are going to feel an urge to do something about it.

That urge is the problem.

Finals week is when families start adding things. An extra kicking session in the backyard. A talk about focus. A better breakfast, a new pair of boots, slightly more advice than usual on the drive to training. Every one of those is well meant, and every one of them tells a ten-year-old the same thing: this week is different, so you need to be different too.

They can’t be different. They’re ten. All you’ve done is move the ground underneath them in the week they most need it to stay still.

Why finals week goes wrong before anyone gets to Saturday

Sport psychologists are fairly consistent on why pre-game routines help kids: it isn’t the routine itself, it’s the repetition. Doing the same things in the same order, week after week, is what turns a warm-up into a signal. The body recognises the pattern and settles.

Which means the routine is only worth anything while it stays the same.

So the week you decide to improve it is the week it stops doing its job. Extra training in finals week doesn’t add skill, because skill doesn’t move in five days. What it does add is a message: the normal amount wasn’t enough. That’s a heavy thing to hand a kid on a Wednesday.

The good version of finals week is boring. Same training, same dinner, same bedtime, same amount of talking about footy as any other week. Which is to say: not much.

The week before: change almost nothing

Three things worth actively protecting.

  1. The normal schedule. If Tuesday training is the usual hour, keep it the usual hour. If your kid has a piano lesson on Thursday, they still have a piano lesson on Thursday. Cancelling other things to “focus on the final” makes the final enormous.
  2. The normal amount of footy talk. If you’d usually ask how training went and then move on, do that. Finals week is when parents start circling back to it at dinner, and kids notice.
  3. The gear. Do not buy new boots. Whatever’s on their feet has been broken in over a season, and the one Saturday you don’t want a blister is this one.

And one thing worth actually doing: get the logistics sorted early. Find out the ground, the time, and where you’re parking, on Wednesday rather than Saturday morning. A calm car trip is worth more than anything you’ll say in it.

The night before: sleep is the one lever worth pulling

If you only change one thing all week, make it bedtime, and make it earlier.

A study led by Matthew Milewski at Children’s Hospital Los Angeles, published in the Journal of Pediatric Orthopaedics, followed 112 teenage athletes across a season. The ones averaging under eight hours of sleep a night were 1.7 times more likely to get injured than the ones who slept more. Sleep was one of the two strongest predictors in the whole study.

That was teenagers, not eight-year-olds, and it was about injury rather than performance. But it points at something worth taking seriously: sleep is doing more work than almost anything else you could add, and it’s the one thing families routinely trade away in a big week.

The night before a final, the useful move is not a pep talk. It’s lights out twenty minutes earlier than usual, phone out of the room, and a completely ordinary evening in between.

They probably won’t sleep brilliantly. Kids rarely do before something they care about. Getting them into bed earlier means the poor sleep still adds up to enough.

Saturday morning, and the ten minutes before they run out

Keep breakfast familiar. This is not the day to introduce porridge to a child who eats Weet-Bix. Whatever they normally eat before a game, two to three hours out, is the right answer, because their stomach already knows it.

Get there early enough that nobody is rushing. Rushed parents make anxious kids, and they do it without saying a word.

Then, in the last few minutes, give them one job. One. Something they control and can actually do.

“Go hard at the first contest.” “Talk to your teammates.” “First one to every ball-up.”

Not “have fun”, which is lovely and means nothing at 9am on a grand final morning. Not “kick a goal”, which is an outcome they can’t control and a way to fail before quarter time. One physical, doable thing gives a nervous brain somewhere to put itself.

Then stop. Say something warm that has nothing to do with the game, and let them go.

What to do if they’re genuinely nervous

Some kids arrive at a final white-faced and quiet. That’s not a warning sign. That’s a kid who cares.

Don’t try to talk them out of it. “Don’t be nervous” has never once worked on anybody, and it adds a second problem: now they’re nervous and they think they shouldn’t be.

Name it as a body thing instead. Their heart is going, their hands are cold, their stomach feels wrong. That’s the body getting ready, and it happens to every player out there including the best one on the ground. Nerves and readiness feel almost identical from the inside, and kids find that genuinely reassuring because it’s true.

Then get them moving. Nerves sit still and get worse. A kick-to-kick in the car park does more than any conversation.

The other thing that steadies a kid before a big game is evidence. Not encouragement, evidence. A kid who can point to what they’ve actually done this season stands in that huddle differently to one who’s just been told they’ll be fine. That’s the whole reason ScorX exists: fifteen games your kid can actually see, so the biggest one isn’t the only one they’re measured by.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do you prepare a child for a footy final?

Mostly by leaving the week alone. Preparation for a final is subtraction rather than addition, because the routine your kid has built over a season only works while it stays the same. Keep training, meals, bedtime and the usual amount of footy talk exactly as they were. Skip the extra kicking sessions, the new boots and the motivational conversations, all of which quietly signal that the normal amount wasn’t enough. Do change one thing: get them to bed twenty minutes earlier the night before, because sleep is the single biggest lever available and it’s the first thing families trade away in a big week. On the morning, keep breakfast familiar, arrive early enough that nobody is rushing, and give them one controllable job before they run out, like going hard at the first contest. Then say something warm that isn’t about footy and let them play.

What should my kid eat before a final?

Whatever they normally eat before a game, two to three hours beforehand. Familiar beats optimal. A final is the worst possible day to test a new breakfast.

Should we do extra training in finals week?

No. Skill doesn’t move in five days, and the extra session mostly communicates that the usual effort wasn’t good enough. Keep the normal training load and let them arrive fresh.

What should I say right before they run out?

One job they control, then something warm that isn’t about the game. “Go hard at the first ball-up” gives a nervous brain a place to land. “Have fun” and “kick a goal” both sound supportive and neither is something they can act on.

What if they’re so nervous they’re not enjoying it?

Name the feeling as a physical thing rather than a problem, because nerves and readiness feel almost the same from the inside and every player out there has some version of it. Then get them moving. A kick in the car park settles a kid faster than a conversation will.

entry.title: The Habits Coaches Notice Most in Kids Who Improve Fastest

link.title: The Habits Coaches Notice Most in Kids Who Improve Fastest

entry.content:
Coaches remember the kid who was warming up before training officially started, more clearly than they remember the kid who kicked the best goal that day. Talent gets noticed in the moment. Habits get noticed over a season.

If you’ve ever asked a coach what actually separates the kids who improve fastest, it’s rarely raw ability. It’s a handful of small, repeatable behaviours that show up week after week, long before the stats do.

Showing up early says more than you’d think

A kid who’s on the field ten minutes before training starts isn’t just being punctual. They’re doing laps, kicking to a mate, getting their body moving before anyone’s blown a whistle. Coaches clock this fast, and not because they’re grading attendance.

It signals something about how the kid feels about being there. There’s a difference between a kid who arrives because a parent dropped them off on time, and a kid who arrives early because they wanted the extra ten minutes. Coaches can tell which one it is within a few weeks.

You don’t need to manufacture this. If your kid is naturally an early arriver, that’s worth naming out loud. “I noticed you were first out there again” lands better than generic praise, because it’s specific and it’s true.

Full effort in the boring drills is the real tell

Anyone can go hard in a match. It’s what a kid does in a repetitive, low-stakes drill. It’s the fifteenth handball in a row, the cone drill nobody’s watching closely that tells a coach how a player actually trains.

Coaches talk about this a lot: the kid who treats a warm-up lap like it’s the last quarter of a final. Not because the drill demands it, but because that’s just how they move. It’s not about being the fastest kid on the track. It’s about not switching off just because the stakes feel low.

This is a genuinely learnable habit, and it’s one of the few things a parent can actually influence without hovering. Kids pick up on whether effort is treated as optional or as the baseline. This mostly comes from what gets noticed and named at home and on the sideline, not from a pep talk before the game.

Leading without being told to

Every junior team has a kid who claps a teammate after a missed shot, or calls out encouragement to the player who’s clearly having a rough quarter, without a coach prompting it. That’s leadership, and it’s got nothing to do with wearing a captain’s armband.

Coaches watch for this specifically because it’s rare and it’s real. A kid can be told to “be a good teammate” a hundred times and it won’t stick the way it does when it’s just who they are on the field. The kids who do this consistently tend to get more responsibility over time. It’s not because a coach decided to fast-track them, but because trust builds the same way habits do: repeatedly, in small moments nobody scripted.

If you want to encourage this in your own kid, the fastest way isn’t a lecture about sportsmanship. It’s pointing out the specific moment you saw it happen. “I saw you check on Jack after he dropped that mark” does more than “be encouraging out there” ever will.

Why these habits matter more than a single good game

A great game is a single data point. A kid who’s early, who trains hard in the boring bits, and who backs up teammates without being asked is showing you a pattern. These patterns are what actually predict whether a kid keeps improving or plateaus.

This is part of why a single stat line from one game can be misleading. A kid can have a quiet game on the scoreboard and still be doing everything right in terms of effort and habits that week. That’s exactly the gap ScorX was built to close. Tracking touches and involvement across a season, not just judging a kid off one bad Saturday, so the pattern is visible instead of guessed at.

How to actually reinforce these habits as a parent

You can’t force a kid to want the extra ten minutes on the field. But you can make it easier for the right things to get noticed and named.

  • Name the behaviour, not the outcome. “You worked hard in that drill” beats “great game” — it tells them what to repeat.
  • Ask about effort, not just result. “How’d training feel today?” opens a different conversation than “did you win?”
  • Don’t wait for the highlight to say something. The car ride home is often about the goal. The habit conversation is better had earlier, closer to when it happened.
  • Let the coach be the one who notices leadership. If a coach mentions your kid checked on a teammate, that lands ten times harder coming from them than from you.

Frequently Asked Questions

What habits do coaches notice most in junior players?

Coaches consistently mention early arrival, full effort in low-stakes drills, and unprompted encouragement of teammates as the habits that stand out most — often more than raw skill or a single standout game.

Can these habits actually be taught, or are some kids just like that?

Both. Some kids arrive with a naturally competitive or conscientious streak, but effort and leadership habits are also shaped by what gets noticed and named consistently at home and on the sideline.

Does showing up early actually matter, or is it just a nice-to-have?

It matters because it’s a visible signal of intent. Coaches use it as an early, low-effort way to gauge how a kid feels about being there, well before performance data tells the same story.

How do I encourage my kid to bring more effort to drills without pressuring them?

Praise the specific effort you saw, not the general outcome. “You went hard on that last set” is more effective and less pressuring than “you need to try harder.”

entry.title: When Should Your Kid Start a Development Plan?

link.title: When Should Your Kid Start a Development Plan?

entry.content:
You’ve probably heard the phrase somewhere — a coach mentioned it at training, another parent dropped it in the group chat, or it turned up in a club email about “player pathways.” Individual development plan. It sounds like something that needs a meeting room and a laminator. It doesn’t.

A development plan in junior sport is really just three things written down: a couple of things your kid is genuinely good at, a couple of things they need to work on, and the specific drills tied to each one. That’s the whole thing. No spreadsheets, no sports scientist, no sit-down with the coach that opens with “so, about Jack’s trajectory.”

They exist to solve one problem: most kids spend training doing generic work — a bit of everything, none of it targeted — when a small amount of focused time on the right thing would move the needle a lot further. A development plan is just what points that time at the two or three things that will actually make the biggest difference, instead of spreading it thin across everything.

So when does your kid actually need one?

Most kids don’t need a formal development plan before about age ten. Somewhere between U12 and U13 — when training gets more structured and the gap between kids starts to actually show on the field — is when a plan earns its place. Before that, the only plan worth having is “kick it, mark it, have fun, go again.”

That’s not a brush-off. It’s what recognised coaching frameworks says too. Most Junior Coaching Curriculums (roughly ages 7 to 12) are built around learning to work as an individual, then in small groups, then as part of a team. It’s only when kids hit Youth Coaching Curriculums, from 13 up, that they flag “a wide spectrum of developmental maturity” — which is a polite way of saying some fourteen-year-olds are built like men and others still look like they’re in Year 6. That gap is exactly where an individual plan starts to matter.

Why ten to twelve is the turning point

Up until about U11, most of what a kid needs is touches, reps, and a coach who lets them have a go. Skills are still general. Everyone’s working on the same basics based on their sport. For AFL it will be kicking, marking and tackling technique.A plan doesn’t add much because the whole team is basically on the same plan.

Around U12, that changes. Training sessions get longer and more structured. Positions start meaning something. And some kids’ effort and some kids’ natural growth spurt start producing very different seasons. That’s not a sign something’s gone wrong. It’s the exact point where a plan pays off, because it gives a kid something specific to work on instead of a vague sense they should “try harder.”

What a plan should actually look like before that age

If your eight-year-old’s development plan is longer than a sentence, it’s too long. At early junior level, the plan is: show up, get a game, enjoy the car ride home. Anything more structured than that risks making training feel like homework, and a kid who feels like footy is homework doesn’t keep playing.

So what goes in an actual development plan?

Strip away the jargon and every good development plan is built from the same two ingredients: strengths and weaknesses, each one paired with a specific drill.

  1. A couple of genuine strengths. Not “he’s a great kid”, but an actual skill. Strong overhead marking. Good closing speed. The point of naming a strength isn’t to hand out a compliment, it’s to pair it with a drill that keeps building on it, so a kid’s best asset doesn’t quietly plateau while everyone focuses on what’s wrong.
  2. A couple of specific weaknesses. Specific enough that a coach could hand over a drill for it tomorrow. “Doesn’t tackle well” is a feeling. “Tends to reach in with one arm instead of wrapping up” is something you can actually train.
  3. A drill for each one. This is the part most plans skip, and it’s the part that matters most. A strength or weakness without a drill attached is just an observation. “Work on your left foot” is an observation. “Ten kicks off the left boot at the start of every training session” is a drill.
  4. A way to check whether the drill’s actually working. Not a feeling — a number, a note, a video clip, something the kid can look back on in six to eight weeks and see moved.

The kid should write the weaknesses on the list, but with some guidance from a coach or parent. A plan a coach or parent writes without ever asking the kid what they think they’re bad at is a to-do list, not a development plan — and kids are usually more accurate about this than adults expect.

What doesn’t need to be in it: disposal counts from every single game, a comparison to teammates, or anything that reads like a performance review. This is development, not monitoring.

Where ScorX fits in

Making sure that focused time actually happens is exactly the gap ScorX’s training module was built to close. We’ve just added development planning into it — so instead of strengths, weaknesses, and drills living in a coach’s notebook or a parent’s head, a kid can set them properly, log against them through the season, and actually see the shift. Not “you played well today.” A number that moves. The full picture of how that works — recording games, measuring athleticism, and building the plan from both — is on the ScorX for athletes page.

A quick example

Say a coach flags two things after a few games: strong overhead marking (strength), and a habit of reaching in with one arm instead of wrapping up the tackle (weakness). The plan pairs each with a drill — extra contested marking reps at training to keep the strength sharp, and a two-arm tackling drill run every session to fix the weakness before it becomes a habit that’s harder to unlearn at fifteen than at eleven.

Six weeks later, the tackle count tells the story on its own. Not “he tried harder.” A number that moved because a specific drill targeted a specific thing.

Frequently Asked Questions

What age should a junior AFL player start a development plan?

Around U12 to U13 is the right window for most kids — roughly when training becomes more structured and individual differences start to show. Before that, focus on participation and enjoyment rather than formal goals.

Do development plans only matter for the “talented” kids?

No — if anything, they matter more for kids who aren’t the most naturally gifted. A plan gives every kid something concrete to improve, rather than leaving progress to whoever developed early or got the most game time.

Who should write the plan — the coach or the parent?

Neither, alone. The best plans start with the kid’s own sense of what they want to work on, with a coach or parent helping shape it into something specific and measurable.

How often should a development plan be updated?

Every six to eight weeks works well for most junior seasons. Long enough to see real change, short enough that one bad game doesn’t derail the whole plan.

What’s the difference between a development plan and just tracking stats?

Stats on their own are just numbers. A development plan gives those numbers a purpose — a named strength or weakness, a specific drill attached to it, and a number that shows whether the drill actually worked.

Do I need a separate drill for every strength and weakness?

Yes, ideally. A weakness without a drill is just an observation — naming it doesn’t fix it. Keep the list short (two or three of each) so every one actually gets a drill, rather than a long list where most items never get worked on.

entry.title: Why Performance Academies Run Testing Days (And What They’re Measuring)

link.title: Why Performance Academies Run Testing Days (And What They’re Measuring)

entry.content:
Testing days exist because coaches can’t compare a hunch to a hunch. When a program has forty kids trying out and eight spots, “he looked quick” isn’t something you can put next to another kid’s “he looked quick” and get a useful answer. A stopwatch can.

What’s actually happening on a testing day?

Usually a run through a handful of standard tests: a sprint over a set distance, a beep test or shuttle run for endurance, a vertical jump, sometimes an agility run through cones. Nothing exotic. The point isn’t the tests themselves, it’s that every kid does the exact same one, the exact same way, on the exact same day.

That sameness is the whole trick. A coach watching two different games can’t really compare a kid who played in the wet against a kid who played in perfect conditions. A 20-metre sprint on a dry track at 9am removes all of that. Everyone’s compared on the same ground, literally.

Why bother testing at all, if coaches already watch them play?

A few reasons, and none of them are about replacing what a coach sees with their own eyes.

It gives them a number to check against, later. A coach can watch a kid all season and form an opinion. A test gives them a figure they can compare in three months, six months, a year. “He’s dropped half a second off his sprint” is something you can actually track. “He seems faster” is a feeling.

It’s the only fair way to compare kids who’ve never played together. Testing days happen a lot at intake and trial stage, when a program is looking at kids from ten different clubs who’ve never shared a field. Match footage tells you how a kid performs inside their own team. It doesn’t tell you much about how he’d go against a kid from the next suburb over. A shared test does.

It flags physical readiness, not just talent. Some of what gets tested, particularly at older ages, isn’t really about picking the best player. It’s screening for load capacity, movement quality, whether a body’s ready for a heavier training program before it’s handed one. That’s more injury prevention than selection.

It gives every kid the same shot to show something. This one gets missed. A kid who’s quiet on the field, who doesn’t get many touches because of how a game happened to flow that day, gets a clean chance to show his sprint time is genuinely elite. Testing can surface a kid a coach might have otherwise walked past.

Does a fast time or a big jump mean a kid “makes it”?

No, and any program that treats it that way is doing it wrong. A testing day measures a handful of physical qualities on one morning. It doesn’t measure decision-making, how a kid reads the play, whether he backs up hard when he hasn’t got the ball, or what he’s like at training in week nine when it’s cold and nobody’s watching. Coaches who’ve been doing this a long time will tell you the same thing: the data narrows the group, it doesn’t pick the team. What happens on the field over months still does most of the deciding.

It’s also worth saying plainly: one test on one day is a snapshot, not a verdict. Kids peak at wildly different ages. A kid who tests average at eleven can be the fastest kid in the squad at fourteen. Programs that are any good know this and build it into how they read the numbers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to prepare my child for a testing day?

Not in any special way. Turning up rested, having eaten, and having done normal training in the weeks before is enough. Cramming sprint drills the week of a test won’t change much and can leave a kid tired instead of sharp.

What’s a good sprint or jump result for a junior athlete?

It depends heavily on age, growth stage, and which sport, so there’s no single number worth chasing. What matters more is a kid’s own result compared to their own result six months earlier.

Are testing days only for elite pathway programs?

Mostly, yes. Community clubs generally don’t run formal testing days, and don’t need to. It’s mainly academies, state programs, and higher-level trial processes that use them, because they’re comparing kids who’ve never trained together.

Should my child feel anxious about a testing day?

It helps to frame it as one input among many, not a pass or fail moment. A coach weighing testing data alongside months of what they’ve actually seen on the field is a coach doing it properly.

Can a bad testing day undo a good season?

Not with a program worth being part of. One number on one morning doesn’t erase what a coach has watched all year. If a program is making decisions purely off a single test day, that’s worth noticing.

entry.title: What Penalty Shootouts Teach Kids About Staying Calm Under Pressure

link.title: What Penalty Shootouts Teach Kids About Staying Calm Under Pressure

entry.content:
The thing everyone gets wrong about a penalty shootout is thinking it’s about nerve. It’s not. It’s about routine, and routine is something your kid can actually copy.

Watch the walk-up next time one happens. Same number of steps. Same spot for the ball. Same breath before the run-up. The player isn’t fighting nerves in that moment. They did that already, weeks ago, somewhere you didn’t see.

Why the shootout looks like courage but is really preparation

A kid watching a shootout sees a grown adult calmly slot the ball into the corner with the whole world watching, and assumes that’s just what brave people do under pressure. It’s not bravery. It’s a routine so well worn that the body knows what to do even when the brain is panicking.

That’s worth saying out loud to your kid, because it’s the opposite of what they usually think. They think composed people don’t feel nervous. Composed people feel exactly as nervous as everyone else. They’ve just rehearsed the next move so many times it runs without needing calm to switch on.

The actual skill is built away from the cameras

Every shootout you’ll watch this fortnight was decided, in part, weeks or months earlier — in training, in front of nobody, taking the same kick over and over until it stopped being a decision and became a habit.

That’s the same idea behind a kid who’s nailed their free-throw routine, or a netball player who’s practised the same set shot a hundred times before she ever takes it in a real game with the score close. The composure people admire afterwards isn’t a personality trait. It’s a rehearsed sequence with the nerves still attached.

What to ask your kid instead of “wasn’t that brave”

Skip the praise of the result. Ask about the process instead.

“What do you reckon he does, every single time, before he kicks it?” Let them notice it’s the same routine, not a different brave decision each time.

“Do you reckon he was actually calm, or just used to it?” This is the question that does the real work. It separates “calm” from “practised,” which is the distinction that actually helps your kid before their next big moment — a grand final, a tryout, a tight quarter with the ball in their hands and ten seconds on the clock.

A small thing to try before their next big moment

If your kid has a free kick, a penalty, a set shot, a serve — anything with a pause before the action — help them build a routine and stick to it. Same three things, every single time. It doesn’t need to be elaborate. A breath, a look at the target, a fixed number of steps.

The point isn’t the specific routine. It’s that it’s the same one every time, so on the day it matters, their body already knows what comes next and their brain doesn’t have to invent it under pressure.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do penalty takers look so calm under pressure?

Most of what looks like calm is actually a well-rehearsed routine. The player has taken that same kick hundreds of times in training, so on the day it matters their body runs the sequence automatically, even while they’re genuinely nervous.

How can I help my child handle pressure in their own sport?

Help them build a small, repeatable routine for moments with a pause before the action — a free throw, a set shot, a penalty. The same sequence every time reduces the number of decisions they have to make under pressure.

Is staying calm under pressure something kids are just born with?

No. It’s mostly a trained response built through repetition, not a fixed personality trait. Kids who seem naturally composed have usually just rehearsed the moment more than it looks like from the outside.

What’s a good age to start teaching pressure routines?

Any age where a kid takes a set shot, free kick, or serve with a pause beforehand. Even a simple two-step routine — same breath, same look at the target — gives a ten-year-old something concrete to hold onto.

entry.title: What Elimination Football Teaches Kids About Big Games

link.title: What Elimination Football Teaches Kids About Big Games

entry.content:
From this weekend, every World Cup match is win-or-go-home. That’s a useful thing to point at, because your kid’s grand final works exactly the same way, and they’ve probably never had it explained to them that clearly before.

Group stage football has room to recover. Lose a game, you can still make the knockouts. Elimination football doesn’t have that. One bad ten minutes and the tournament’s over, no matter how good the previous six weeks were.

Most kids playing finals footy, netball, or basketball this season are about to feel that same shift, and most of them don’t have the words for why a normal game suddenly feels heavier.

Why “it’s just another game” doesn’t help

Coaches and parents often try to lower the temperature before a big game by saying it’s just like any other. It isn’t, and kids generally know that, which is why the line doesn’t land. A grand final has the same rules as round three, but it doesn’t have the same forgiveness built in. There’s no next week to fix it.

The World Cup gives you a cleaner way to say this. Point out that the teams who lost their first or second group game still had a path forward. They could lose once and recover. From the round of 32, that path’s gone. One mistake at the wrong moment and it’s over, no matter what they did to get there.

Ask your kid: “Do you reckon the players feel different walking out for a knockout game compared to a group game?” They’ll say yes. Ask why. Most kids land on something close to the truth without you needing to supply it: there’s no next chance to fix it.

The actual skill: playing the same way regardless of the stakes

The best teams in a knockout round don’t play differently because of the stakes. They try to play exactly like they did in the group stage with the same shape, same patience, same process and let the result take care of itself. The teams that get caught out are usually the ones who can feel the stakes changing their decisions mid-game.

This is the single most useful idea to hand a kid before a final. Not “just relax,” which is impossible to act on, but “play it like round three.” Same routines before the game. Same warm-up. Same first touch, same first tackle, same instructions from the coach. The stakes are different. The way they play shouldn’t be.

What changes for coaches running a finals week

If you’re coaching a side into finals, the World Cup gives you a low-stakes way to raise this with your group before it becomes their problem. A ten-minute conversation about what’s different about knockout football. By using a match they’ve already watched, not their own upcoming game, it gets the idea into their heads without making the conversation feel like it’s about them specifically.

Keep training the same in the week before a final. Same drills, same warm-up structure, same rotations talk. The temptation is to do something different because the game feels different. Resist it. Consistency in the lead-up is the thing that actually helps a nervous group, not a special pep talk on the day.

What to say in the car on the way to a final

Skip “good luck” and skip “just have fun,” which kids have heard so many times it’s stopped meaning anything. Try something closer to what the knockout teams are actually doing: “Play it exactly like you played last week. That’s all that’s different. Everything else stays the same.”

That sentence does more work than it looks like, because it gives a nervous kid something to do with their hands, so to speak. A specific, familiar instruction is calming in a way that “relax” never manages to be.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I help my child handle nerves before a grand final?

Tell them to play it exactly like a normal game, with the same warm-up and routines they’ve used all season. Consistency in preparation is more calming than reassurance, because it gives them something concrete to focus on rather than the size of the occasion.

Why do knockout or elimination games feel different to kids than regular season games?

Because the margin for error disappears. In a normal game, a mistake can be fixed next week. In an elimination game, there’s no next week, and kids pick up on that shift even if they can’t always explain it.

Should I talk to my kid about the pressure before a big game, or avoid the topic?

Naming it briefly and matter-of-factly tends to help more than avoiding it. Kids usually know the game feels different. Pretending otherwise can make them feel like nobody’s acknowledging what they’re going through.

How should coaches change training before a final?

Mostly, they shouldn’t. Keeping the structure, warm-up, and rotations consistent with a normal training week is more useful than introducing something new, which can unintentionally signal to the team that this game requires a different approach.

ScorX is free to download. Track the season, not just the final. Most development happens long before the game that gets remembered.
